basis.text: The licence looked up is ABC Type 48 (on-sale general, public premises), as stated in the description.

filing_playbook.action: Confirm the zoning pathway in writing with the San Francisco Planning Department: whether a 14,139 sq ft bar use requires a Conditional Use Authorization under Planning Code § 744 (use size 6,000+ sq ft), and whether the space has a legal nonconforming use on file.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: State the address (895 O'Farrell St, parcel 0717/013), the proposed use (bar, ABC Type 48, full liquor, no entertainment, closes by midnight, 14,139 sq ft), and ask whether the use-size trigger at 6,000 sq ft applies and requires a CUA hearing. Ask the planner to check the parcel history for any legal nonconforming bar use that would make this a continuation rather than a new use. Request the answer in writing (email or a zoning determination letter) before filing any applications or signing a lease contingent on permits.

filing_playbook.action: Obtain a California Seller's Permit from the Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA) and arrange workers' compensation insurance from a licensed carrier or State Fund.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Register online at the CDTFA portal for a seller's permit (free, often issued same day) to collect sales tax on food and drinks. CDTFA may request a security deposit depending on projected sales. Then quote workers' compensation insurance (mandatory from the first employee) through a broker or State Compensation Insurance Fund; restaurant class codes typically run 2–6% of payroll. ABC will not issue a liquor license until the seller's permit exists, and city permits ask for proof of workers' comp, so complete both before the ABC application.

filing_playbook.action: Schedule and pass the Department of Public Health pre-opening inspection after DBI plan check approval, then apply for the Health Permit to Operate.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: After DPH approves the plans, schedule a pre-final inspection at ~80% construction complete and a final inspection when the kitchen is fully installed, finishes are sealed, hand sinks and hot water are operational, and a certified food protection manager is on staff. Book each inspection with your plan reviewer at least two weeks ahead. The permit is issued after the final inspection confirms the facility matches the approved plans. The FY 2026–27 fee is $470 for the application with initial inspection, and the annual license fee is $0 for bars through 2026–28. Reinspections are $276/hour, so walk the space against the DPH checklist a week before the final inspection to avoid a failed inspection that pushes opening by 2–3 weeks.

filing_playbook.action: Complete Responsible Beverage Service (RBS) training for all alcohol servers and managers, and enroll at least one owner or employee in a food safety manager certification course.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Every alcohol server and manager must complete RBS certification within 60 days of hire under AB 1221: register on the ABC RBS Portal ($3), complete an approved course ($10–25), and pass the exam. Keep the certification list on site for ABC inspections. At least one person must pass an ANSI-accredited food safety certification exam (ServSafe, Prometric, NRFSP, 360training; $100–250, 1–14 days) within 60 days of opening; health inspectors ask for the certificate at the pre-opening inspection. All employees who handle food must obtain a California Food Handler Card within 30 days of hire ($7–15, online course takes ~2 hours, valid 3 years).

timeline_cost.notes: No time or cost range is given because the zoning answer is not established: Planning Code § 744 requires a Conditional Use Authorization for uses of 6,000 square feet or more in the NCD-Lower Polk Street district, and 14,139 square feet is over that threshold, yet the supplied pathway indicates no CUA is required for this concept. The first step of the playbook is to confirm the zoning pathway in writing with the Planning Department before any applications are filed or costs are incurred. If a CUA is required, the timeline would be 120–300 days and the application fee $3,100–15,000 (Planning Commission hearing, 300-foot notice, environmental review, and a 30-day appeal period), plus 90–240 days and $17,000–450,000 for the ABC Type 48 license transfer (including escrow, posting, and a Public Convenience or Necessity determination for the over-concentrated census tract), plus 14–120 days and $800–15,000 for the building permit with change of use, plus 21–60 days and $828–2,500 for the DPH plan check, plus 14–45 days and $470–1,000 for the health permit to operate, for a total of roughly 259–725 days and $21,798–483,500 government costs (not including the license purchase price of $100k–450k). If no CUA is required, remove the 120–300 days and $3,100–15,000 from the sum. The alcohol license row is insufficient information because the transaction type (new, transfer from within the tract, or transfer from outside) is not stated, and the entitlement path does not include the ABC license, so no time or cost is given here.

records_summary: 895 O'Farrell St is zoned NCD-Lower Polk Street where a restaurant is principally permitted on the first story. The records show no prior applications or ABC licenses at this exact address or parcel (0717/013), so the existing use is not established by the public record. The immediate area is densely served: 25 registered food/drink businesses within 500 ft, 6 active ABC on-sale licenses within 500 ft, and 45 within 1,000 ft. The few dated use decisions nearby (N = 3 in the last 10 years within 1,000 ft, too few for a rate) show 2 approvals and 1 withdrawal, with most nearby restaurant and ABC referrals routinely approved as principally permitted uses in both the NCD-Lower Polk Street and adjacent RC-4 districts.
data_gaps: No records establish what 895 O'Farrell St is currently used as, so whether adding alcohol service is truly an intensification or a change of use cannot be confirmed.
ABC license conditions are not exposed in the dataset, so operating restrictions on the six nearby on-sale licenses are unknown.
The census tract's undue-concentration status for ABC purposes is not directly shown; only a proxy count of licenses within 500 ft.
No hearing transcripts or decision texts are available for the three dated use-decision cases, so reasons for the one withdrawal are unknown.
The 14,139 sq ft stated in the profile is unusually large for a restaurant with 5 employees and limited cooking; the records do not clarify the building's use or tenancy.
